description: Separate (not fully independent: the reader is a Claude model like the writer, and Sonnet is also a judge) check of the study's reworded and negated claims by a reader who did not write them (Claude Sonnet, 2026-10-02). check=reworded: same meaning? check=negated: is the negated claim clearly not supported by the cited source? The reader was given, for every negated claim, the source sentences an earlier run quoted as proof of the original claim, and ruled on those sentences; it did not open the full source files. A reworded claim it ruled to change the meaning was fixed before publication; one more rewording (pots/t7), which this reader ruled the same, was changed after a later content reader found it kept only one of two readings. Each fix is recorded on its row under fix_applied, and the copies were rebuilt from the fixed wording.

rows.original: sufficiently advanced AI could gain a "decisive strategic advantage"
rows.variant: sufficiently advanced AI could obtain a "decisive strategic advantage"
rows.why: gain and obtain are interchangeable here; the hedge 'could' and the quoted term are kept.

rows.original: in 2024, institutions based in the United States produced 40 of the year's notable AI
rows.variant: in 2024, United States-based institutions produced 40 of the year's notable AI
rows.why: Only the word order of the same description changed; year, figure and country are kept.

rows.original: and quantifiable, and is made through an extremely concentrated supply chain.
rows.variant: and quantifiable, and its production runs through an extremely concentrated supply chain.
rows.why: 'is made through' becomes 'its production runs through'; 'extremely concentrated supply chain' is intact.

rows.original: United States hosted roughly three-quarters of the world's AI-supercomputer performance
rows.variant: United States was home to roughly three-quarters of the world's AI-supercomputer performance
rows.why: 'hosted' and 'was home to' mean the same; the figure and the hedge 'roughly' are kept.

rows.original: the share of income paid as wages falls and an increasing share
rows.variant: the wage share of income declines and a growing share
rows.why: Falls/declines and increasing/growing are equivalent; direction of both changes is kept.

rows.original: energy, land, materials, and built capacity — become the binding constraint
rows.variant: energy, land, materials, and built capacity — come to be the binding constraint
rows.why: 'become' and 'come to be' are equivalent; all four inputs are kept.

rows.original: great divergence" in economic performance between countries rather than only within them.
rows.variant: great divergence" in economic performance across countries, not only inside them.
rows.why: 'between countries rather than only within' and 'across countries, not only inside them' keep both the between-country divergence and the within-country part.

rows.original: restricts access to its most capable models on a tiered, country-by-country basis
rows.variant: limits access to its most capable models country by country, on a tiered basis
rows.why: Restrict/limit, and tiered and country-by-country are both kept.

rows.original: and in Hungary foreign investors came to control roughly 90% of
rows.variant: and in Hungary foreign investors ended up controlling roughly 90% of
rows.why: 'came to control' and 'ended up controlling' are equivalent; figure and hedge kept.

rows.original: around 70% of foundational AI models since 2017 have been built there
rows.variant: around 70% of foundational AI models since 2017 have been developed there
rows.why: built/developed equivalent; the source itself says 'developed'.

rows.original: and they already trail those models — by about four
rows.variant: and they are already behind those models — by about four
rows.why: trail and are behind are equivalent; 'already' and 'about four' kept.

rows.original: off news for users across Australia and later removed it from its platforms in Canada altogether
rows.variant: off news for users throughout Australia and later removed it entirely from its platforms in Canada
rows.why: across/throughout and altogether/entirely are equivalent; the later timing and both countries are kept.

rows.original: both of which the major frontier-AI firms now supply to governments through dedicated
rows.variant: both of which the major frontier-AI firms now provide to governments through dedicated
rows.why: supply/provide equivalent.

rows.original: was released only through a restricted programme to trusted United States
rows.variant: was made available only through a restricted programme to trusted United States
rows.why: 'released only through' and 'made available only through' keep the exclusivity.

rows.original: the United States ordered Anthropic to bar all foreign nationals from Fable 5 and Mythos 5
rows.variant: Anthropic was ordered by the United States to bar all foreign nationals from Fable 5 and Mythos 5
rows.why: Active turned passive; actor, target, scope ('all foreign nationals') and both models kept.

rows.original: took the episode as proof of "why Europe must strengthen its technological sovereignty"
rows.variant: treated the episode as proof of "why Europe must strengthen its technological sovereignty"
rows.why: 'took ... as' and 'treated ... as' equivalent; quote kept.

rows.original: was more persuasive than a human opponent in
rows.variant: outperformed a human opponent at persuasion in
rows.why: 'more persuasive than' becomes 'outperformed at persuasion'; the following 'roughly two-thirds of the matched debates' is unchanged.

rows.original: successive model generation has been rated more persuasive than the one before
rows.variant: successive model generation has been judged more persuasive than its predecessor
rows.why: rated/judged and 'the one before'/'its predecessor' equivalent.

rows.original: preference by more than is typically achieved by conventional video advertising
rows.variant: preference by more than conventional video advertising typically achieves
rows.why: Same comparison, same 'typically' hedge, restructured.

rows.original: OpenAI reports having disrupted more than twenty covert influence operations
rows.variant: OpenAI says it disrupted more than twenty covert influence operations
rows.why: reports having / says it equivalent; figure kept.

rows.original: Because the provider alone decides who may use its models — and already restricts their use in political
rows.variant: Because only the provider decides who may use its models — and it already restricts their use in political
rows.why: 'alone decides' and 'only the provider decides' mean the same; 'already restricts' kept.

rows.original: the data of everyday digital life has itself become a
rows.variant: the data generated by everyday digital life has itself turned into a
rows.why: Minor: 'the data of everyday digital life' becomes 'the data generated by' it, which adds a claim about how the data arises (a narrower reading than the original).

fix_applied.new_variant: the data of everyday digital life has itself turned into a
fix_applied.note: Fixed before publication by the Claude Code session that prepared the study, not by the separate reader: 'of' is kept as in the original, so the only change left is 'become' to 'turned into'.

rows.original: an AI system improving its own capabilities in an accelerating cycle, the "intelligence explosion" first
rows.variant: an AI system enhancing its own capabilities in an accelerating loop, the "intelligence explosion" first
rows.why: improving/enhancing and cycle/loop equivalent; 'first' and the quoted term kept.

rows.original: labour and judgement by AI erodes society's dependence on human participation

rows.original: tend to be less accountable to them and to invest less in them
rows.variant: tend to answer less to them and to invest less in them
rows.why: 'less accountable to' and 'answer less to' equivalent; 'tend' hedge kept.

rows.original: "independent and controllable" AI stack an explicit national goal.
rows.variant: "independent and controllable" AI stack an explicitly stated national goal.
rows.why: explicit/explicitly stated equivalent.

rows.original: world's total and a 95% self-sufficiency target for staple grains.
rows.variant: world's total and a target of 95% self-sufficiency in staple grains.

rows.original: Self-sufficiency has a cost in lost income, China still lags at the frontier of
rows.variant: Self-sufficiency costs lost income, China still trails at the frontier of

rows.original: nearly all the poorest, are net importers of food
rows.variant: nearly all the poorest, import more food than they export
rows.why: 'net importer' is defined as importing more than exporting; 'nearly all' kept.

rows.original: the failure of entitlement that Sen identified.
rows.variant: the entitlement failure identified by Sen.
rows.why: Same concept and attribution.

rows.original: the share of its people who were undernourished rose from about 3% to roughly
rows.variant: the undernourished share of its people climbed from about 3% to roughly

rows.original: environmental corners cut to avoid finishing second.
rows.variant: environmental corners cut so as not to finish second.

rows.original: develops the case for an international agreement to halt frontier development until the
rows.variant: makes the case for an international agreement halting frontier development until the

rows.original: politics then turns into a contest over
rows.variant: politics then becomes a contest over
rows.why: turns into/becomes equivalent.

rows.original: United States policy while average citizens have little or none
rows.variant: United States policy, whereas average citizens have little or none
rows.why: while/whereas equivalent.

rows.original: argue that a race to artificial superintelligence defeats itself.
rows.variant: argue that racing to artificial superintelligence is self-defeating.
rows.why: defeats itself / is self-defeating equivalent.

rows.original: in which any bid for unilateral dominance invites
rows.variant: under which any bid for unilateral dominance provokes
rows.why: Minor nuance: 'invites' (makes likely) versus 'provokes' (triggers) is slightly stronger, but 'any bid' and the result (pre-emptive sabotage) are kept; the source says 'is met with'.

rows.original: natural resources become a main driver of economic outcomes
rows.variant: natural resources become one of the main drivers of economic outcomes
rows.why: 'a main driver' and 'one of the main drivers' are equivalent.

rows.original: International Energy Agency projects data-centre electricity demand more than doubling by 2030
rows.variant: International Energy Agency expects data-centre electricity demand to more than double by 2030
rows.why: projects/expects equivalent; 'more than' and year kept.

rows.original: but that current output is capped near 500,000 by
rows.variant: but that current output is limited to around 500,000 by
rows.why: capped near / limited to around equivalent; figure kept.

rows.original: optimistic case for which Altman is a prominent voice.
rows.variant: optimistic case, with Altman as one of its prominent voices.
rows.why: 'a prominent voice' and 'one of its prominent voices' equivalent.

rows.original: The same entitlement failure that turns economic collapse into famine applies to a cheap surplus
rows.variant: The same failure of entitlement that converts economic collapse into famine applies to a cheap surplus

rows.original: technology spreads slowly and unevenly: the lag between a technology's invention and its
rows.variant: technology diffuses slowly and unevenly: the lag between a technology's invention and its
rows.why: spreads/diffuses equivalent.

rows.original: the case for preparing for them now rather than deferring them to
rows.variant: the argument for preparing for them now instead of deferring them to
rows.why: case/argument and rather than/instead of equivalent.

rows.original: Weathered biotite demonstrates superior cesium sorption, often by two orders of magnitude, compared to other clay minerals like illite, smectite, kaolinite, and halloysite
rows.variant: Compared to other clay minerals like illite, smectite, kaolinite, and halloysite, weathered biotite shows superior cesium sorption, often by two orders of magnitude
rows.why: Clauses reordered; every fact and 'often' kept.

rows.original: Montmorillonite also shows high adsorption capacity, outperforming illite and kaolinite
rows.variant: Montmorillonite also has a high adsorption capacity, performing better than illite and kaolinite
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: Specific bentonite types, which contain montmorillonite, are effective: Kunipia-F bentonite is superior to SiO2 , natural Ca-bentonite has a higher capacity than Na-bentonite , and inorganic modified Na-bentonite shows high adsorption under alkaline conditions
rows.variant: Specific bentonite types containing montmorillonite are effective: Kunipia-F bentonite outperforms SiO2 , natural Ca-bentonite has a greater capacity than Na-bentonite , and inorganic modified Na-bentonite adsorbs strongly under alkaline conditions
rows.why: Synonym swaps only; all three comparisons and the alkaline condition kept.

rows.original: Molybdenum vanadate loaded bentonite also enhances cesium removal
rows.variant: Cesium removal is also enhanced by molybdenum vanadate loaded bentonite
rows.why: Active turned passive.

rows.original: Glauconite exhibits higher sorption than bentonite , and acid-activated kaolinite significantly improves natural kaolinite's efficiency
rows.variant: Glauconite shows greater sorption than bentonite , and acid activation of kaolinite significantly improves natural kaolinite's efficiency
rows.why: Equivalent; 'significantly' kept.

rows.original: While zeolite shows the highest overall sorption among minerals , weathered biotite appears to be the best clay sorption material.
rows.variant: While zeolite has the highest overall sorption of all minerals , weathered biotite appears to be the best clay material for sorption.
rows.why: 'among minerals' becomes 'of all minerals', same superlative scope; hedge 'appears to be' kept.

rows.original: Engelmann et al. report evidence that chimpanzees also prepare for multiple possible outcomes and suggest that they too represent exclusive-OR relations.
rows.variant: Engelmann et al. present evidence that chimpanzees also prepare for multiple possible outcomes, and propose that they too represent exclusive-OR relations.
rows.why: report/present and suggest/propose are close; 'propose' is marginally more assertive than 'suggest' but the hedged-claim reading is intact.

rows.original: in which an experimenter drops a reward into an inverted Y-shaped tube with two exits, such that a participant must simultaneously cover both exits with one hand each to guarantee successfully catching it
rows.variant: in which an experimenter drops a reward into an inverted Y-shaped tube with two exits, so that a participant has to cover both exits at the same time, one hand on each, to be sure of catching it
rows.why: Equivalent task description.

rows.original: Across our studies, we have found little evidence that non-human primates insightfully prepare for mutually exclusive possibilities in this simple context
rows.variant: In our studies, we have found little evidence that non-human primates prepare insightfully for mutually exclusive possibilities in this simple context
rows.why: 'Across our studies' becomes 'In our studies': a very slight loss of the 'pooled over several studies' flavour, same meaning for a checker.

rows.original: we found that three chimpanzees, one orangutan and one capuchin monkey spontaneously covered both exits despite never seeing that behaviour before.
rows.variant: we found that three chimpanzees, one orangutan and one capuchin monkey covered both exits spontaneously although they had never seen that behaviour before.
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: Each of these five individuals regressed to covering one exit on subsequent trials.
rows.variant: On subsequent trials, each of these five individuals regressed to covering one exit.
rows.why: Only the order of the clauses changed.

rows.original: chimpanzees spontaneously covered two exits on 24.4% of trials, seven times more often than when only one reward was unpredictably dropped into one of the two mutually exclusive tubes
rows.variant: chimpanzees covered two exits spontaneously on 24.4% of trials, a rate seven times higher than when only one reward was unpredictably dropped into one of the two mutually exclusive tubes
rows.why: Equivalent; figures and condition kept.

rows.original: The three individuals who learned to consistently cover both exits towards the end of the simultaneous trials (i.e. passing 90–100% of the final 10 trials) subsequently passed only 17–58% of mutually exclusive trials in a supplementary experiment.
rows.variant: The three individuals who learned to cover both exits consistently near the end of the simultaneous trials (i.e. passing 90–100% of the final 10 trials) went on to pass only 17–58% of mutually exclusive trials in a supplementary experiment.
rows.why: All figures and 'only' kept.

rows.original: The apes had to cover both exits to guarantee a reward in the mutually exclusive trials, but could simply cover one exit to guarantee a reward in the simultaneous trials
rows.variant: In the mutually exclusive trials the apes had to cover both exits to guarantee a reward, but in the simultaneous trials they could simply cover one exit to guarantee a reward
rows.why: Trial-type assignment preserved.

rows.original: The data indicate that the primates’ trouble with preparing for mutually exclusive possibilities was at least partly in their minds and not simply in their hands.
rows.variant: According to the data, the primates’ difficulty in preparing for mutually exclusive possibilities was at least partly in their minds and not simply in their hands.
rows.why: Equivalent; 'at least partly' kept.

rows.original: Three individuals had to be excluded [from Engelmann et al.'s study] because the target behaviour was too difficult for them
rows.variant: Three individuals had to be excluded [from Engelmann et al.'s study], as they found the target behaviour too difficult
rows.why: Equivalent; number and cause kept.

rows.original: The preregistration states that the remaining chimpanzees were given up to three attempts per trial if they failed to balance either platform and that trials were excluded if they did not.
rows.variant: According to the preregistration, the remaining chimpanzees received up to three attempts per trial if they failed to balance either platform, and trials were excluded if they did not.
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: On their first trial, 7/16 chimpanzees balanced both platforms in the control condition and 8/16 did so in the test condition.
rows.variant: In the control condition 7/16 chimpanzees balanced both platforms on their first trial, and in the test condition 8/16 did so.
rows.why: Figures stay assigned to the correct conditions.

rows.original: research on clinical versus statistical prediction has demonstrated that algorithms make more accurate predictions than humans in many domains
rows.variant: research comparing clinical and statistical prediction has shown that algorithms predict more accurately than humans in many domains
rows.why: Equivalent; 'in many domains' kept.

rows.original: In the 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, 169 superforecasters and domain experts forecast benchmarks resolving by 2024–2025
rows.variant: In the 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, benchmarks resolving by 2024–2025 were forecast by 169 superforecasters and domain experts
rows.why: Active turned passive; figures and year kept.

rows.original: Respondents underestimated AI progress, especially superforecasters — for three standard AI benchmarks (MATH, MMLU, and QuALITY), domain experts assigned probabilities of 21.4%, 25.0%, and 43.5% respectively to outcomes achieved by end of 2024, while superforecasters were even more pessimistic at 9.3%, 7.2%, and 20.1%
rows.variant: Respondents, especially superforecasters, underestimated AI progress — for three standard AI benchmarks (MATH, MMLU, and QuALITY), domain experts gave probabilities of 21.4%, 25.0%, and 43.5% respectively to outcomes achieved by end of 2024, while superforecasters were even more pessimistic at 9.3%, 7.2%, and 20.1%
rows.why: Figures in the same order; 'especially superforecasters' still modifies the underestimation.

rows.original: AI systems achieved gold-level Olympiad performance to which domain experts assigned only 8.6% and superforecasters a mere 2.3% probability; overall superforecasters assigned an average probability of just 9.7% to observed outcomes across four AI benchmarks, versus 24.6% from domain experts
rows.variant: AI systems reached a gold-level Olympiad performance to which domain experts gave only 8.6% and superforecasters a mere 2.3% probability; across four AI benchmarks, superforecasters overall gave observed outcomes an average probability of just 9.7%, versus 24.6% from domain experts
rows.why: All figures and groups kept.

rows.original: The same cohort simultaneously overestimated improvements in climate technology — the opposite directional error
rows.variant: At the same time, the same cohort overestimated improvements in climate technology — an error in the opposite direction
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: Steinhardt's parallel exercise found that the AI experts had similar medians but were overconfident in the tails, while the superforecasters systematically underpredicted progress, and generalist crowd forecasters fared worst
rows.variant: Steinhardt's parallel exercise found that the AI experts had similar medians but were overconfident in the tails, whereas the superforecasters systematically predicted too little progress, and generalist crowd forecasters did worst
rows.why: underpredicted = predicted too little; rest unchanged.

rows.original: FRI's ongoing expert panel shows this persisting into 2025–2026: recent benchmark performance suggests the median expert is substantially underestimating the progress of development of SOTA AI systems
rows.variant: FRI's ongoing expert panel shows this continuing into 2025–2026: recent benchmark performance suggests that the median expert substantially underestimates the progress of development of SOTA AI systems
rows.why: Equivalent; 'suggests' hedge kept.

rows.original: AI capability growth, by contrast, is discontinuous and compute-driven, leaving no comparable historical baseline
rows.variant: By contrast, AI capability growth is compute-driven and discontinuous, so there is no comparable historical baseline
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: Tellingly, individual forecasters' near-term performance was statistically indistinguishable from simple algorithms — a "no-change" forecast and trend extrapolation — and there was no statistically significant correlation between near-term accuracy and long-term existential-risk forecasts
rows.variant: Tellingly, the near-term performance of individual forecasters could not be statistically distinguished from simple algorithms — a "no-change" forecast and trend extrapolation — and near-term accuracy had no statistically significant correlation with long-term existential-risk forecasts
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: In an adversarial-collaboration study, "concerned" domain experts predicted a 20% chance of AI-caused existential catastrophe by 2100, while "skeptical" participants — mainly superforecasters — predicted 0.12%, and neither side substantially updated toward the other's views
rows.variant: In an adversarial-collaboration study, "concerned" domain experts put the chance of AI-caused existential catastrophe by 2100 at 20%, while "skeptical" participants — mainly superforecasters — put it at 0.12%, and neither side substantially updated toward the other's views
rows.why: Figures and groups unchanged.

rows.original: existential AI risk is dominated by epistemic uncertainty (unknown mechanism) rather than aleatoric uncertainty (a stable random process)
rows.variant: epistemic uncertainty (unknown mechanism), not aleatoric uncertainty (a stable random process), dominates existential AI risk
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: In 1212 Frederick II's Golden Bull of Sicily confirmed hereditary kingship for Přemysl Otakar I and reduced Bohemia's tribute and military duties.
rows.variant: In 1212 Frederick II's Golden Bull of Sicily confirmed Přemysl Otakar I's hereditary kingship and lowered Bohemia's tribute and military duties.
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: philological analysis dates that clause precisely to the disputed election of Rudolf of Habsburg on 1 October 1273
rows.variant: philological analysis dates that clause exactly to Rudolf of Habsburg's disputed election on 1 October 1273
rows.why: precisely/exactly; date and event kept.

rows.original: That episode fits a wider pattern in which German identity hardened through contrast with Slavic neighbours
rows.variant: That episode matches a broader pattern in which German identity hardened by contrast with Slavic neighbours
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: By 1273 Ottokar ruled Austria, Styria, Carinthia and Carniola besides Bohemia and Moravia, the wealthiest prince in the empire, so electors chose the obscure Rudolf of Habsburg to check that dominance.
rows.variant: By 1273 Ottokar, the wealthiest prince in the empire, ruled Austria, Styria, Carinthia and Carniola in addition to Bohemia and Moravia, so electors chose the obscure Rudolf of Habsburg to check that dominance.
rows.why: The apposition 'wealthiest prince' is moved next to Ottokar, which is how the original reads; all lands and the purpose kept.

rows.original: after Rudolf died in 1291 the electors bypassed his son Albert for Adolf of Nassau, explicitly to forestall a hereditary Habsburg dynasty.
rows.variant: after Rudolf's death in 1291 the electors passed over his son Albert in favour of Adolf of Nassau, explicitly to forestall a hereditary Habsburg dynasty.
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: Bohemian kingship also legitimized itself through dynastic and sacral tradition centred on Saint Wenceslas's cult
rows.variant: Bohemian kingship also drew its legitimacy from dynastic and sacral tradition centred on the cult of Saint Wenceslas
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: decay fungi need moisture, oxygen, warmth, and a food source together, and the exposed end grain atop a post is where rainwater collects longest
rows.variant: decay fungi require moisture, oxygen, warmth, and a food source at the same time, and rainwater collects longest on the exposed end grain at the top of a post
rows.why: Equivalent; 'longest' and all four requirements kept.

rows.original: a cross-culturally recurring practice of placing charged objects at a dwelling's vulnerable edges
rows.variant: a practice, recurring across cultures, of placing charged objects at the vulnerable edges of a dwelling
rows.why: Equivalent.

rows.original: Early modern English witch bottles were stoneware or glass jugs filled with pins, nails, and bodily fluids, then heated and concealed near hearths and thresholds, attested from roughly the 1650s to at least 1705.
rows.variant: Early modern English witch bottles were stoneware or glass jugs that were filled with pins, nails, and bodily fluids, then heated and hidden near hearths and thresholds; they are attested from roughly the 1650s to at least 1705.
rows.why: Dates, materials and hedges kept.

rows.original: The popular claim that these bottles were preventive charms barring witches is not well supported by the surviving texts, which frame them chiefly as a cure applied once bewitchment was already suspected.
rows.variant: The surviving texts give little support to the popular claim that these bottles were preventive charms barring witches, framing them chiefly as a cure applied once bewitchment was already suspected.
rows.why: 'not well supported' and 'give little support' equivalent; cure framing kept.

rows.original: A related Finnish tradition of hiding animal bones, coins, and tools in thresholds shows the same anxiety, with witchcraft fears more pronounced in densely built towns than in looser settlements.
rows.variant: A related Finnish tradition of hiding animal bones, coins, and tools in thresholds reflects the same anxiety, with fears of witchcraft more pronounced in densely built towns than in looser settlements.
rows.why: shows/reflects equivalent.

rows.original: English museum surveys report a comparable concealment pattern at hearths and doorways.
rows.variant: Surveys by English museums report a comparable pattern of concealment at hearths and doorways.
rows.why: Equivalent.

fix_applied.new_variant: English museum surveys report a comparable pattern of concealment at hearths and doorways.
fix_applied.note: Changed before publication by the Claude Code session that prepared the study, after a later content reader pointed out that 'Surveys by English museums' keeps only one of the two readings of 'English museum surveys' (surveys made by museums), while the source, a survey of bottles held in museums and other collections, fits the other reading (surveys of what museums hold). The new wording keeps 'English museum surveys' as in the original, so the only change left is 'concealment pattern' to 'pattern of concealment'. The separate reader's ruling on this row was made on the earlier wording.

rows.original: in 2024, institutions based in the United States produced 40 of the year's notable AI
rows.variant: in 2024, institutions based in the United States produced none of the year's notable AI
rows.why: Source: 'In 2024, U.S.- based institutions produced 40 notable AI models'; 'none' is contradicted.

rows.original: and quantifiable, and is made through an extremely concentrated supply chain.
rows.variant: and quantifiable, and is made through a widely dispersed supply chain.
rows.why: Source: 'AI computing hardware is tangible and produced using an extremely concentrated supply chain'; 'widely dispersed' is the opposite.

rows.original: United States hosted roughly three-quarters of the world's AI-supercomputer performance
rows.variant: United States hosted only a small fraction of the world's AI-supercomputer performance
rows.why: Source: 'the United States contains about three-quarters of global GPU cluster performance' (74.5%).

rows.original: the share of income paid as wages falls and an increasing share
rows.variant: the share of income paid as wages rises and a decreasing share
rows.why: Source (Korinek and Trammell): 'the labor share again falls to 0'; the reversal is contradicted.

rows.original: great divergence" in economic performance between countries rather than only within them.
rows.variant: great divergence" in economic performance only within countries rather than between them.
rows.why: UNDP piece is titled 'Why AI May Widen Inequality Between Countries' and says AI may 'drive nations apart'; the source stresses between-country divergence.

rows.original: restricts access to its most capable models on a tiered, country-by-country basis
rows.variant: grants all countries equal, untiered access to its most capable models
rows.why: Source: 'Access to the most capable models is throttled by default' and 'The Frontier Inference Services Rule (FISR) is a country-based licensing regime.'

rows.original: around 70% of foundational AI models since 2017 have been built there
rows.variant: only a small minority of foundational AI models since 2017 have been built there
rows.why: Draghi: 'Around 70% of foundational AI models have been developed in the US since 2017'.

rows.original: and they already trail those models — by about four
rows.variant: and they already lead those models — by about four
rows.why: Epoch: 'the most capable open-weight models have lagged frontier closed models by an average of four months'.

rows.original: took the episode as proof of "why Europe must strengthen its technological sovereignty"
rows.variant: denied that the episode showed "why Europe must strengthen its technological sovereignty"
rows.why: Agence Europe: 'The Commission also believes that this case illustrates once again "why Europe must strengthen its technological sovereignty"'.

rows.original: was more persuasive than a human opponent in
rows.variant: was less persuasive than a human opponent in
rows.why: Source: 'personalized GPT-4 opponents were more persuasive than human opponents' 64.4% of the time.

rows.original: successive model generation has been rated more persuasive than the one before
rows.variant: successive model generation has been rated less persuasive than the one before
rows.why: Anthropic: 'each successive model generation is more persuasive than the previous'.

rows.original: an AI system improving its own capabilities in an accelerating cycle, the "intelligence explosion" first
rows.variant: an AI system improving its own capabilities in an accelerating cycle, the "intelligence explosion", which was never
rows.why: Good's own paper: 'there would then unquestionably be an "intelligence explosion"'; combined with the unchanged tail 'described by Good', the claim that he never described it is contradicted. Note the variant relies on the unchanged tail of the sentence to read correctly.

rows.original: labour and judgement by AI erodes society's dependence on human participation
rows.variant: labour and judgement by AI deepens society's dependence on human participation
rows.why: Kulveit et al. describe 'an effectively irreversible loss of human influence' and a shift in the citizen-state relationship; the source says the opposite of deepening dependence.

rows.original: "independent and controllable" AI stack an explicit national goal.
rows.variant: "independent and controllable" AI stack a goal it has explicitly abandoned.
rows.why: MERICS: Xi 'urged a nationwide mobilization to achieve self-reliance ... by building an "independent and controllable" ecosystem'; nothing about abandonment.

rows.original: environmental corners cut to avoid finishing second.
rows.variant: environmental standards kept intact even at the cost of finishing second.
rows.why: Armstrong et al.: teams are 'incentivised to finish first – by skimping on safety precautions if need be' and a 'race to the bottom'. Nothing supports standards kept intact.

rows.original: develops the case for an international agreement to halt frontier development until the
rows.variant: develops the case against any international agreement to halt frontier development until the
rows.why: MIRI: 'This would be a global Halt on frontier AI development ... a coordinated and collectively enforced moratorium'; the team argues for, not against.

rows.original: United States policy while average citizens have little or none
rows.variant: United States policy, and average citizens have just as much
rows.why: Gilens and Page: average citizens 'have little or no independent influence'.

rows.original: argue that a race to artificial superintelligence defeats itself.
rows.variant: argue that a race to artificial superintelligence does not defeat itself.
rows.why: The source title is 'Why a Race to Artificial Superintelligence is Self-Defeating'.

rows.original: in which any bid for unilateral dominance invites
rows.variant: in which no bid for unilateral dominance invites
rows.why: Hendrycks et al.: 'any state's aggressive bid for unilateral AI dominance is met with preventive sabotage by rivals'.

rows.original: natural resources become a main driver of economic outcomes
rows.variant: natural resources cease to matter for economic outcomes
rows.why: Korinek and Trammell: if other factors 'become scarce relative to effective capital plus labor' they drive wages down; scarce natural resources matter. Erdil and Besiroglu name 'land, energy and capital' as bottlenecks. (The quoted sentence supports the original only indirectly, but none supports 'cease to matter'.)

rows.original: International Energy Agency projects data-centre electricity demand more than doubling by 2030
rows.variant: International Energy Agency projects data-centre electricity demand falling by 2030
rows.why: IEA: 'Data centre electricity consumption is set to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030'.

rows.original: but that current output is capped near 500,000 by
rows.variant: but that current output faces no cap near 500,000 from
rows.why: Epoch: 'current output caps production at roughly 500,000 humanoids per year'.

rows.original: optimistic case for which Altman is a prominent voice.
rows.variant: optimistic case that Altman rejects.
rows.why: Altman's essay argues AI will bring 'dramatically more wealth to go around' and everything becoming half as expensive; he advocates, not rejects.

rows.original: the case for preparing for them now rather than deferring them to
rows.variant: the case for deferring them, rather than preparing for them now, to
rows.why: MacAskill and Moorhouse: 'And that suggests we should be preparing now.'

rows.original: Weathered biotite demonstrates superior cesium sorption, often by two orders of magnitude, compared to other clay minerals like illite, smectite, kaolinite, and halloysite
rows.variant: Weathered biotite demonstrates inferior cesium sorption, often by two orders of magnitude, compared to other clay minerals like illite, smectite, kaolinite, and halloysite
rows.why: Source: WB 'sorbed 137Cs far more than the other clay minerals'; 'about two orders of magnitude higher'.

rows.original: Montmorillonite also shows high adsorption capacity, outperforming illite and kaolinite
rows.variant: Montmorillonite also shows low adsorption capacity, underperforming illite and kaolinite
rows.why: Source: 'montmorillonite adsorbed more Cs than illite and kaolinite under all tested conditions'.

rows.original: Molybdenum vanadate loaded bentonite also enhances cesium removal
rows.variant: Molybdenum vanadate loaded bentonite does not enhance cesium removal
rows.why: Source: 'the modification of bentonite with molybdenum vanadate enhances the sorption properties of Cs(I) ions'.

rows.original: Glauconite exhibits higher sorption than bentonite , and acid-activated kaolinite significantly improves natural kaolinite's efficiency
rows.variant: Glauconite exhibits lower sorption than bentonite , and acid-activated kaolinite significantly reduces natural kaolinite's efficiency
rows.why: Sources: 'The higher sorption capacity of glauconite in comparison with bentonite' and 'adsorption efficiency of Cs+ ion by acid-activated kaolinite clay showed much higher compared with natural kaolinite'.

rows.original: Engelmann et al. report evidence that chimpanzees also prepare for multiple possible outcomes and suggest that they too represent exclusive-OR relations.
rows.variant: Engelmann et al. report evidence that chimpanzees do not prepare for multiple possible outcomes and suggest that they do not represent exclusive-OR relations.
rows.why: Source: 'Engelmann et al. report evidence that chimpanzees also prepare for multiple possible outcomes and suggest that they too represent exclusive-OR relations.'

rows.original: in which an experimenter drops a reward into an inverted Y-shaped tube with two exits, such that a participant must simultaneously cover both exits with one hand each to guarantee successfully catching it
rows.variant: in which an experimenter drops a reward into an inverted Y-shaped tube with two exits, such that a participant can guarantee catching it by covering just one exit
rows.why: Source: 'a participant must simultaneously cover both exits with one hand each to guarantee successfully catching it'.

rows.original: Across our studies, we have found little evidence that non-human primates insightfully prepare for mutually exclusive possibilities in this simple context
rows.variant: Across our studies, we have found strong evidence that non-human primates insightfully prepare for mutually exclusive possibilities in this simple context
rows.why: Source: 'we have found little evidence that non-human primates insightfully prepare ...'.

rows.original: we found that three chimpanzees, one orangutan and one capuchin monkey spontaneously covered both exits despite never seeing that behaviour before.
rows.variant: we found that three chimpanzees, one orangutan and one capuchin monkey covered both exits only after seeing that behaviour demonstrated.
rows.why: Source: 'spontaneously covered both exits despite never seeing that behaviour before ... our subjects did not require training or demonstration'.

rows.original: Each of these five individuals regressed to covering one exit on subsequent trials.
rows.variant: Each of these five individuals kept covering both exits on subsequent trials.
rows.why: Source: 'each of these five individuals regressed to covering one exit on subsequent trials'.

rows.original: chimpanzees spontaneously covered two exits on 24.4% of trials, seven times more often than when only one reward was unpredictably dropped into one of the two mutually exclusive tubes
rows.variant: chimpanzees spontaneously covered two exits on 24.4% of trials, seven times less often than when only one reward was unpredictably dropped into one of the two mutually exclusive tubes
rows.why: Source: 24.4% 'seven times more often than' the 3.4% rate in the mutually exclusive condition.

rows.original: The three individuals who learned to consistently cover both exits towards the end of the simultaneous trials (i.e. passing 90–100% of the final 10 trials) subsequently passed only 17–58% of mutually exclusive trials in a supplementary experiment.
rows.variant: The three individuals who learned to consistently cover both exits towards the end of the simultaneous trials (i.e. passing 90–100% of the final 10 trials) subsequently passed all of the mutually exclusive trials in a supplementary experiment.
rows.why: Source: 'subsequently passed only 17–58% of mutually exclusive trials'.

rows.original: The apes had to cover both exits to guarantee a reward in the mutually exclusive trials, but could simply cover one exit to guarantee a reward in the simultaneous trials
rows.variant: The apes could simply cover one exit to guarantee a reward in the mutually exclusive trials, but had to cover both exits to guarantee a reward in the simultaneous trials
rows.why: Source states the opposite assignment of trial types.

rows.original: The data indicate that the primates’ trouble with preparing for mutually exclusive possibilities was at least partly in their minds and not simply in their hands.
rows.variant: The data indicate that the primates’ trouble with preparing for mutually exclusive possibilities was simply in their hands and not in their minds.
rows.why: Source: 'at least partly in their minds and not simply in their hands'.

rows.original: Three individuals had to be excluded [from Engelmann et al.'s study] because the target behaviour was too difficult for them
rows.variant: No individuals had to be excluded [from Engelmann et al.'s study] because the target behaviour was too difficult for them
rows.why: Source: 'too difficult for some chimpanzees, and so three individuals had to be excluded'.

rows.original: The preregistration states that the remaining chimpanzees were given up to three attempts per trial if they failed to balance either platform and that trials were excluded if they did not.
rows.variant: The preregistration states that the remaining chimpanzees were given only one attempt per trial if they failed to balance either platform and that trials were excluded if they did not.
rows.why: Source: 'given up to three attempts per trial'.

rows.original: On their first trial, 7/16 chimpanzees balanced both platforms in the control condition and 8/16 did so in the test condition.
rows.variant: On their first trial, none of the 16 chimpanzees balanced both platforms in either the control or the test condition.
rows.why: Source: '7/16 chimpanzees balanced both platforms in the control condition and 8/16 did so in the test condition'.

rows.original: In the 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, 169 superforecasters and domain experts forecast benchmarks resolving by 2024–2025
rows.variant: In the 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, 169 superforecasters and domain experts declined to forecast benchmarks resolving by 2024–2025
rows.why: Source assesses 'the accuracy of short-term forecasts made during' the XPT by the 169 participants, with probabilities assigned on benchmarks; declining is contradicted.

rows.original: Respondents underestimated AI progress, especially superforecasters — for three standard AI benchmarks (MATH, MMLU, and QuALITY), domain experts assigned probabilities of 21.4%, 25.0%, and 43.5% respectively to outcomes achieved by end of 2024, while superforecasters were even more pessimistic at 9.3%, 7.2%, and 20.1%
rows.variant: Respondents overestimated AI progress, especially superforecasters — for three standard AI benchmarks (MATH, MMLU, and QuALITY), domain experts assigned probabilities of 21.4%, 25.0%, and 43.5% respectively to outcomes achieved by end of 2024, while superforecasters were even more optimistic at 9.3%, 7.2%, and 20.1%
rows.why: Source: 'XPT participants significantly underestimated the pace of AI advancement' and superforecasters 'even more pessimistic'.

rows.original: AI systems achieved gold-level Olympiad performance to which domain experts assigned only 8.6% and superforecasters a mere 2.3% probability; overall superforecasters assigned an average probability of just 9.7% to observed outcomes across four AI benchmarks, versus 24.6% from domain experts
rows.variant: AI systems fell short of gold-level Olympiad performance to which domain experts assigned only 8.6% and superforecasters a mere 2.3% probability; overall superforecasters assigned an average probability of just 9.7% to observed outcomes across four AI benchmarks, versus 24.6% from domain experts
rows.why: Source: 'AI systems achieved gold-level performance in July 2025'.

rows.original: The same cohort simultaneously overestimated improvements in climate technology — the opposite directional error
rows.variant: The same cohort simultaneously underestimated improvements in climate technology — the same directional error
rows.why: Source: 'Climate technology progress was overestimated.'

rows.original: Steinhardt's parallel exercise found that the AI experts had similar medians but were overconfident in the tails, while the superforecasters systematically underpredicted progress, and generalist crowd forecasters fared worst
rows.variant: Steinhardt's parallel exercise found that the AI experts had similar medians but were overconfident in the tails, while the superforecasters systematically overpredicted progress, and generalist crowd forecasters fared worst
rows.why: Source: 'They (probably) systematically underpredicted progress' and superforecasters 'are too bearish on progress'.

rows.original: FRI's ongoing expert panel shows this persisting into 2025–2026: recent benchmark performance suggests the median expert is substantially underestimating the progress of development of SOTA AI systems
rows.variant: FRI's ongoing expert panel shows this persisting into 2025–2026: recent benchmark performance suggests the median expert is substantially overestimating the progress of development of SOTA AI systems
rows.why: Source: 'the median expert is substantially underestimating the progress of development of SOTA AI systems'.

rows.original: Tellingly, individual forecasters' near-term performance was statistically indistinguishable from simple algorithms — a "no-change" forecast and trend extrapolation — and there was no statistically significant correlation between near-term accuracy and long-term existential-risk forecasts
rows.variant: Tellingly, individual forecasters' near-term performance clearly outperformed simple algorithms — a "no-change" forecast and trend extrapolation — and there was no statistically significant correlation between near-term accuracy and long-term existential-risk forecasts
rows.why: Source: 'individual forecasters' performance was not statistically distinguishable from two simple algorithms'; 'differences ... were small and not statistically significant'.

rows.original: In an adversarial-collaboration study, "concerned" domain experts predicted a 20% chance of AI-caused existential catastrophe by 2100, while "skeptical" participants — mainly superforecasters — predicted 0.12%, and neither side substantially updated toward the other's views
rows.variant: In an adversarial-collaboration study, "concerned" domain experts predicted a 20% chance of AI-caused existential catastrophe by 2100, while "skeptical" participants — mainly superforecasters — predicted 0.12%, and both sides substantially updated toward the other's views
rows.why: Source: 'Neither the concerned nor the skeptics substantially updated toward the other's views'.

rows.original: In 1212 Frederick II's Golden Bull of Sicily confirmed hereditary kingship for Přemysl Otakar I and reduced Bohemia's tribute and military duties.
rows.variant: In 1212 Frederick II's Golden Bull of Sicily revoked hereditary kingship for Přemysl Otakar I and reduced Bohemia's tribute and military duties.
rows.why: Source: 'Ottokar and his successors would rule the Czech lands hereditarily and free of any payment'.

rows.original: By 1273 Ottokar ruled Austria, Styria, Carinthia and Carniola besides Bohemia and Moravia, the wealthiest prince in the empire, so electors chose the obscure Rudolf of Habsburg to check that dominance.
rows.variant: By 1273 Ottokar ruled Austria, Styria, Carinthia and Carniola besides Bohemia and Moravia, the poorest prince in the empire, so electors chose the obscure Rudolf of Habsburg to support that dominance.
rows.why: Source: Ottokar's 'seemingly unstoppable rise was felt to be progressing at too rapid a pace by the other electors'; supporting his dominance is contradicted, and 'poorest' has no backing.

rows.original: after Rudolf died in 1291 the electors bypassed his son Albert for Adolf of Nassau, explicitly to forestall a hereditary Habsburg dynasty.
rows.variant: after Rudolf died in 1291 the electors chose his son Albert over Adolf of Nassau, explicitly to secure a hereditary Habsburg dynasty.
rows.why: Source: 'The electors chose not Albrecht but Adolf of Nassau ..., hoping to nip the emergence of a royal Habsburg dynasty in the bud.'

rows.original: The popular claim that these bottles were preventive charms barring witches is not well supported by the surviving texts, which frame them chiefly as a cure applied once bewitchment was already suspected.
rows.variant: The popular claim that these bottles were preventive charms barring witches is well supported by the surviving texts, which frame them chiefly as a protection set up before any bewitchment was suspected.
rows.why: Source: 'no known primary texts describe witch-bottles as protective objects; instead, they wholly substantiate that this was a curative practice'.

rows.original: A related Finnish tradition of hiding animal bones, coins, and tools in thresholds shows the same anxiety, with witchcraft fears more pronounced in densely built towns than in looser settlements.
rows.variant: A related Finnish tradition of hiding animal bones, coins, and tools in thresholds shows the same anxiety, with witchcraft fears less pronounced in densely built towns than in looser settlements.
rows.why: Source: 'concerns about envious witchcraft must have been more pronounced in densely built towns and group villages than in the looser settlements'.
